- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially in early-to-mid horizon.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model underestimates downside risk; increase early forecast lows and avoid sharp upward spikes.
- Model often overreacts to sentiment spikes — if sentiment jumps to 1.00, forecast may overshoot by 20–50% in 1–3 day horizon; apply dampening factor to high sentiment spikes.
- Mean reversion is strong in 30-day horizon — if forecast is >2.5x historical mean, reduce by 15–30% unless sentiment supports sustained trend.
- If sentiment history shows alternating highs/lows (e.g., 0.67, 0.33, 0.67…), model tends to misalign with true volatility — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment cycle, not linear trend.
- In low-sentiment periods (e.g., 0.33 or below), model often underestimates true price drops — add 10–20% buffer to downward forecasts.
- Overshoots after sentiment spikes are common in 10–15 day horizon — apply “lag correction”: reduce forecast by 10–25% at 10-day mark if sentiment peaked 5–7 days prior.
